newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria chooses between currency board, high rate.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria chooses between currency board, high rate.

text.p: Bulgaria must choose between adopting a currency board system or sustaining high interest rates as part of monetary restrictions to resolve its grave economic crisis, Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said on Thursday.
"Two alternative stabilisation packages are offered. Which of them is more or less risky should be decided through political consensus," he told reporters.

Under a currency board - a system introduced by some countries to boost credibility in their currencies - the amount of national currency in circulation must be matched exactly by hard currency reserves.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) says adopting a such a board would stabilise Bulgaria's currency, curb inflation and boost economic growth.
On Wednesday, the central bank said it opposed the proposal, calling it "a risky experiment".
"The other option is seeking macroeconomic stabilisation by continuing to fund the budget deficit and maintaining monetary restrictions through high rates," said Kostov.

A currency board system is less risky, Kostov said. It would require amendment of several laws which would deprive the central bank of the usual tools of monetary management, such as market interventions and interest rates.
The central bank would completely stop funding the budget deficit and refinancing of commercial banks would be drastically reduced, said Kostov.

The amount of levs in circulation, including commercial banks' minimum reserve deposits in the central bank totalling 169 billion levs would have to be matched with the country's foreign exchange reserves.

Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) forex reserves stood at $540 million and the country would also have to collateralise its gold, said Kostov. He did not elaborate on whether the all of the country's gold would be collateralised or only some 4.5 tonnes kept in banks abroad.
Delayed structural reforms and a stagnant economy have pressured the lev to 249 to the dollar now from around 70 in January.
In a bid to stabilise the lev, the central bank raised the central interest rate to a record-high 300 percent in September. It is currently 180 percent.
High rates drain funds which could have been used for other priorities or in the real economy, instead they create a vicious circle of accruing deficit, devaluation and inflation, said the IMF.
The current option is less suitable for countries with such big domestic debt as Bulgaria.
The Fund has asked Bulgaria's parliamentary groups to decide whether they would support a currency board system by next week. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
